source_text: Sed est quaedam eiusmodi species in facto et in uerbo bis acuta et infesta utrimque, licet tibi blandiatur, quasi uacet in utroque, dum factum non uidetur, quia dictum non tenetur. pecuniam de ethnicis mutuantes sub pignoribus fiduciati iurati cauent et se negant; se scire uolunt scilicet tempus persecutionis et locus tribunalis et persona praesidis. praescribit Christus non esse iurandum. scripsi, inquit, sed nihil dixi: lingua, non littera occidit. hic ego naturam et conscientiam aduoco: naturam, quia nihil potest manus scribere, etiamsi lingua in dictando cessat immobilis et quieta, quod non anima dictauerit; quamquam et ipsi linguae anima dictauerit aut a se conceptum aut ab alio traditum. iam, ne dicatur, alius dictauit; hic conscientiam appello, an quod alius dictauit anima suscipiat et siue comitante siue residente lingua ad manum transmittat. et bene, quod in animo et conscientia delinqui dominus dixit. si, inquit, concupiscentia uel malitia in cor hominis ascenderit, pro facto teneris. cauisti igitur, quod in cor tuum plane ascendit, quod neque ignorasse te contendere potes neque noluisse. nam cum caueres, scisti, cum scires, utique uoluisti; et est tam facto quam cogitatu. nec potes leuiore crimine maius excludere, ut dicas falsum plane effici cauendo quod non facis. tamen non negaui, quia non iuraui. quin immo, etsi nihil tale fecisses, sic tamen dicereris deierare, fecisse si consenseris. non ualet tacita uox in stilo et mutus in litteris sonus. at enim Zacharias temporali uocis orbatione multatus cum animo conlocutus linguam inritam transit, cum manibus suis a corde dictat et nomen filii sine ore pronuntiat: loquitur in stilo, auditur in cera manus omni sono clarior, littera omni ore uocalior. quaere, an dixerit qui dixisse compertus est. dominum oremus, ne qua nos eiusmodi contractus necessitas circumsistat et, si ita euenerit, det fratribus operandi copiam uel nobis abrumpendae omnis necessitatis constantiam, ne illae litterae negatrices uicariae oris nostri in die iudicii aduersus nos proferantur signatae signis non iam aduocatorum, sed angelorum.
thought_title: The written denial is as guilty as the spoken one
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that even a written denial of faith, such as a Christian signing a pledge when borrowing money from pagans, is a real denial and therefore idolatry.
pass_a_gloss: But there is a certain kind of this sort in deed and in word, two-edged and dangerous on both sides, although it flatters you, as if it were free in both, while the deed is not seen, because the word is not held. Those borrowing money from pagans, bound by pledges, sworn, give security and deny themselves; they want to know, of course, the time of persecution and the place of the tribunal and the person of the governor. Christ prescribes that one must not swear. I wrote, he says, but I said nothing: the tongue, not the letter, kills. Here I call nature and conscience as witnesses: nature, because the hand can write nothing, even if the tongue in dictating rests motionless and quiet, which the soul has not dictated; although the soul has dictated it either to the tongue itself, either a thing conceived by itself or a thing handed over by another. Now, lest it be said, another dictated it; here I appeal to conscience, whether the soul receives what another dictated and transmits it to the hand, whether the tongue accompanies or rests. And well, that the Lord said that one sins in the mind and conscience. If, he says, desire or malice has ascended into the heart of a man, you are held as for the deed. You have given security, therefore, that which has plainly ascended into your heart, which you can contend neither that you did not know nor that you did not want. For when you gave security, you knew; when you knew, you certainly wanted; and it is as much in deed as in thought. Nor can you exclude the greater by the lesser crime, so that you say that what you do not do is plainly made false by giving security. Nevertheless I did not deny, because I did not swear. Nay rather, even if you had done no such thing, still you would be said to swear falsely, if you have consented to its being done. The silent voice in the pen has no force, and the mute sound in letters has no force. But indeed Zechariah, punished with temporary loss of voice, conversed with his mind, passed over his useless tongue, dictated from his heart with his own hands and announces the name of his son without his mouth: he speaks in the pen, he is heard in the wax, the hand clearer than every sound, the letter more vocal than every mouth. Ask whether he has spoken who has been found to have spoken. Let us pray the Lord that no necessity of this kind of contract surround us and, if it so happens, that he give brothers the opportunity of working or us the constancy of breaking off every necessity, lest those denying letters, substitutes for our mouth, be brought forth against us on the day of judgment, signed with signs no longer of advocates, but of angels.

pass_b_english: But there is a kind of case, in deed and in word, that is two-edged and dangerous on both sides. It flatters you, as if it were harmless in either respect, as if the deed is not seen because the word is not held against you. When we borrow money from pagans, bound by pledges, we give security in writing under oath and deny ourselves. The pagans, of course, want to know the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor. Christ prescribes that one must not swear. "I wrote," someone says, "but I said nothing. The tongue, not the letter, kills."

Here I call on nature and conscience. Nature, because the hand can write nothing, even if the tongue rests motionless and quiet while dictating, that the soul has not dictated. Though the soul has dictated to the tongue itself, either something conceived by itself or handed over by another. Now, lest someone say, "Another dictated it," here I appeal to conscience: whether the soul accepts what another dictated and transmits it to the hand, whether the tongue accompanies it or rests. And rightly did the Lord say that sin is committed in the mind and conscience. "If desire or malice has ascended into the heart of a man," He says, "you are held as for the deed."

You have therefore given security for what has plainly ascended into your heart, which you cannot claim either not to have known or not to have willed. For when you gave security, you knew. When you knew, you certainly willed it. And it holds both as deed and as thought. Nor can you exclude the greater charge by a lesser one, saying that what you do not do is plainly made false by giving security. "Still, I did not deny, because I did not swear." On the contrary, even if you had done nothing of the sort, you would still be said to swear falsely if you consented to having done it. A voice silent in the pen still speaks, and a sound mute in letters still sounds.

But Zechariah, punished with temporary loss of voice, conversed with his mind while his tongue was useless. He dictated with his own hands from his heart and announced his son's name without his mouth (Luke 1:63). He speaks in the pen, he is heard in the wax, a hand clearer than any sound, a letter more vocal than any mouth. Ask whether he spoke who has been found to have spoken.

Let us pray the Lord that no necessity of this kind of contract surrounds us, and if it should happen, that He grant our brothers the means to work, or grant us the steadfastness to break off every necessity, so that those denying letters, substitutes for our mouth, may not be brought out against us on the day of judgment, sealed with signs no longer of accusers but of angels.

problems.quote: "If desire or malice has ascended into the heart of a man," He says, "you are held as for the deed" (Matthew 5:28)
problems.source_quote: si, inquit, concupiscentia vel malitia in cor hominis ascenderit, pro facto teneris.
problems.why: The passage is not a citation of Matthew 5:28; the verse does not contain this wording.
problems.fix: "If desire or malice has ascended into the heart of a man," He says, "you are held as for the deed"
problems.ruling: Matthew 5:28 concerns lustful looking; source 'concupiscentia vel malitia in cor ascenderit, pro facto teneris' is not that verse; wrong reference misleads reader.

edits.old: you are held as for the deed" (Matthew 5:28).
edits.new: you are held as for the deed."

fixed: Removed the incorrect Scripture citation (Matthew 5:28); the source words 'si, inquit, concupiscentia vel malitia in cor hominis ascenderit, pro facto teneris' are not a quotation of Matthew 5:28.

problems.quote: A silent voice in the pen has no force, nor does a mute sound in written letters
problems.fix: Change to 'A voice silent in the pen still speaks, and a sound mute in letters still sounds'.

problems.quote: sealed with signs no longer of advocates but of angels
A silent voice in the pen has no force, nor does a mute sound in written letters.
problems.why: The sentence seems to contradict the argument: Tertullian is arguing written denial DOES have force.
problems.fix: Rewrite to clarify: 'A silent voice in the pen is not without force, nor is a mute sound in written letters.'

problems.quote: They want to know, of course, the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.
problems.why: The sentence is unclear: who are 'they' and why do they want to know these things? Context suggests pagan lenders demanding information.
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'The pagans, of course, want to know the time of persecution, the tribunal's location, and the governor's identity.'

fixed: The source 'non ualet tacita uox in stilo et mutus in litteris sonus' means the silent voice in the pen and the mute sound in letters do have force, so the English 'has no force' misstates the source; changed to 'still speaks' and 'still sounds'.

The source 'signatae signis non iam aduocatorum, sed angelorum' uses 'aduocatorum', which in this context means accusers or advocates against us at judgment, not legal advocates; changed to 'accusers'.

The source 'se scire uolunt scilicet tempus persecutionis et locus tribunalis et persona praesidis' refers to the pagans who want to know these details, so 'They' was ambiguous; changed to 'The pagans'.

last_rejected.quote: When we borrow money from pagans, bound by pledges, sworn, we give security in writing and deny ourselves.
last_rejected.source_quote: pecuniam de ethnicis mutuantes sub pignoribus fiduciati iurati cauent et se negant
last_rejected.why: 'et se negant' means 'and deny themselves' (i.e. deny Christ), not 'deny ourselves'; subject is third person, not first.
last_rejected.fix: When they borrow money from pagans, bound by pledges, sworn, they give security in writing and deny themselves.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin says “cauent et se negant” (they provide security and deny themselves); English “deny ourselves” matches; “in writing” is added but not a core meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: They want to know, of course, the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.
last_rejected.source_quote: se scire uolunt scilicet tempus persecutionis et locus tribunalis et persona praesidis
last_rejected.why: 'se scire uolunt' means 'they want to be known' (i.e. they make known), not 'they want to know'; the pagans demand to know these details.
last_rejected.fix: They want it known, of course—the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.
last_rejected.ruling: “se scire volunt” is best read as “they want to know”; translation reflects that, not “they want to be known.”
